# Resettable Injection Training Device

## Overview

The resettable injection training device is a reusable apparatus designed for medical training purposes, allowing repeated simulation of injection procedures while maintaining safety features that protect users from inadvertent contact with the injection simulation component. The device comprises four primary elements: a main body, a slidable plunger, an injection simulation member, and a retractable and extendable shield mechanism.

## Structural Components

The device's body serves as the primary housing structure, providing the framework within which the other components operate. The plunger is configured to slide within or along the body, mimicking the actuation motion of an actual injection device. The injection simulation member represents the needle or injection point component used for training purposes, while the shield functions as a protective barrier that can move between retracted and extended positions relative to this simulation member.

## Pre-Use Configuration

Prior to use, the shield is designed to be releasably locked in a retracted position. This retracted state exposes the injection simulation member, allowing the device to be used for its intended training purpose. The locking mechanism holds the shield securely in this retracted configuration through the engagement of dedicated locking surfaces, ensuring the shield does not prematurely extend during use and interfere with the training exercise.

## Post-Use Safety Mechanism

Following use of the device, the shield automatically transitions from its retracted position to an extended position, moving over and covering the injection simulation member. This automatic extension serves a critical safety function, preventing any subsequent contact with the injection simulation member once the training exercise has been completed. This feature is particularly important in training environments where multiple users or repeated demonstrations may occur, as it minimizes the risk of accidental contact between users and the simulated injection point.

## Reset Functionality

The device is engineered for repeated use through a straightforward reset mechanism. To reset the device, force is applied to the distal end of the shield, causing it to move back into the retracted position. As the shield retracts, the locking surfaces re-engage, securing the shield in place and preparing the device for another training cycle. This reset process restores the device to its pre-use configuration, with the injection simulation member once again exposed and ready for use.

## Release Mechanism

The shield is released from its locked, retracted position through a specific actuation sequence: moving the plunger toward the distal end of the body. This plunger movement causes the locking surfaces to disengage from one another, releasing the shield from its retracted state. Once disengaged, the shield is free to extend over the injection simulation member, triggering the safety covering function described above. This release mechanism ensures that the shield's protective extension is directly linked to the completion of the simulated injection action, providing an intuitive and reliable safety response.

## Summary

Through the coordinated interaction of these components—the body, plunger, injection simulation member, and shield—the device provides a robust, reusable training tool. The locking and release mechanisms work in tandem to ensure the shield remains appropriately positioned throughout the use cycle: retracted and locked before use, automatically extended and protective after use, and easily resettable for subsequent training sessions.

# Injection Training Device with Resettable Retractable Shield Mechanism

## Background and Field of the Invention

Medical training devices that simulate injection procedures are essential tools for educating healthcare professionals, nursing students, and other medical personnel in proper injection techniques. Traditional training approaches have relied heavily on single-use disposable syringes fitted with training needles or simulation members, which, while functional, present significant limitations in terms of cost-effectiveness, environmental sustainability, and practical classroom or clinical training scenarios where repeated demonstrations are necessary.

A persistent challenge in the design of injection training devices has been the need to balance realistic simulation of the injection experience with adequate safety measures to prevent accidental needle-stick injuries or contact with the injection simulation member during training exercises. Many existing devices either lack adequate safety shielding mechanisms or, when such mechanisms are present, are designed for single-use only, requiring disposal after each training session. This creates substantial ongoing costs for educational institutions and healthcare training facilities, while also generating unnecessary medical waste.

Furthermore, existing retractable shield mechanisms in the medical device field have generally been engineered for single-use safety syringes intended for actual patient injections, where a permanent, non-reversible locking of the shield in the extended position is not only acceptable but required as a safety feature to prevent reuse of a contaminated needle. These single-use mechanisms are fundamentally unsuited for training applications, where the same device must be safely and reliably used multiple times by different trainees or during repeated practice sessions.

## Summary of the Invention

The present invention addresses these shortcomings by providing a reusable injection training device incorporating a resettable retractable shield mechanism specifically designed for repeated safe use in educational and training contexts. Unlike conventional single-use safety syringes, the device of the present invention employs a novel locking arrangement that allows the protective shield to automatically extend and lock over the injection simulation member following each simulated injection, thereby preventing inadvertent contact with the member, while also permitting the shield to be manually reset to its retracted, ready-to-use position through the deliberate application of distal force.

The device generally comprises three primary interacting components: a body member, a plunger member slidably disposed within or in relation to the body, and a shield member configured to travel along an axis relative to the injection simulation member. Each of these components includes specifically configured locking surfaces, protrusions, detents, or complementary engagement features that interact with one another in a sequential and controlled manner as the device is manipulated through its use cycle.

In operation, when the plunger is depressed to simulate an injection, the shield member—initially held in a retracted position that exposes the injection simulation member—is released from its retracted locking engagement as the plunger and body interact through their respective locking surfaces. This release allows a biasing element, such as a spring, to drive the shield member distally along the body, extending it to fully cover and enclose the injection simulation member. As the shield reaches its fully extended position, a second set of locking surfaces on the shield and body engage one another, creating a secure lock that prevents the shield from being inadvertently pushed back to expose the simulation member, thereby ensuring that trainees and instructors are protected from accidental contact once the simulated injection has been completed.

A key inventive aspect of this device lies in the mechanism by which the shield can be intentionally reset to its initial, retracted configuration in preparation for a subsequent training session. Rather than being permanently locked in the extended position as would be the case in a single-use disposable safety syringe, the shield mechanism of the present invention is designed such that the application of a controlled distal force—applied by the user against the shield itself, typically by pressing the shield against a surface—causes the locking surfaces to disengage from their locked configuration. This action allows the shield to be moved proximally back into its retracted position, where it re-engages with the initial locking surfaces on the body or plunger, thereby resetting the device for reuse.

## Detailed Description of Preferred Embodiments

In a preferred embodiment, the body of the training device is formed as an elongated hollow structure, sized and shaped to resemble a conventional syringe barrel, thereby providing a realistic tactile and visual training experience. The body includes an interior channel or bore along which the plunger member travels axially. The plunger is fitted with a plunger rod and a distal engagement portion that interacts with corresponding structures on the interior of the body, such as ribs, flanges, or detents, which serve as the locking surfaces responsible for controlling the shield's behavior.

The shield member, which surrounds a portion of the body and is capable of sliding axially relative to it, is fitted over the injection simulation member—which may take the form of a blunt or rubber-tipped needle simulation feature, rather than an actual sharp needle, to further enhance safety during training exercises. The shield is maintained in its initial retracted position, exposing the simulation member, by way of a first locking engagement between corresponding surfaces on the shield and the body. This locking engagement is designed to be robust enough to withstand normal handling forces during training setup, yet capable of being released upon the specific sequence of actions associated with simulating an injection.

Internally, a biasing mechanism, most preferably a coil spring disposed within the body or between the body and shield, is maintained in a compressed or loaded state while the shield is in its retracted position. When the locking engagement between the shield and body is released—triggered by the depression of the plunger to a certain point within the body, whereupon a locking surface on the plunger interacts with and disengages a corresponding surface on the shield or an intermediate locking component—the stored energy in the biasing mechanism is released, driving the shield distally along the body toward and beyond the distal tip of the injection simulation member.

As the shield reaches the end of its distal travel, fully enclosing the simulation member, a second locking engagement occurs between locking surfaces on the shield and the body. This second locking engagement is configured to resist proximal movement of the shield under normal handling forces, effectively securing the shield in its protective, extended position and preventing accidental exposure of the simulation member following the simulated injection.

To reset the device, the user applies a distal force to the shield, such as by pressing the distal end of the shield against a flat surface, such as a tabletop or training pad. This action causes the locking surfaces engaged in the second locking arrangement to flex, deflect, or otherwise disengage in a manner that permits the shield to be moved proximally relative to the body. As the shield is moved proximally, the plunger is correspondingly reset to its initial, undepressed position, and the biasing mechanism is recompressed or reloaded. Continued proximal movement of the shield results in re-engagement of the first locking surfaces, thereby returning the shield to its original retracted position and preparing the device for another simulated injection cycle.

The locking surfaces themselves may be embodied in a variety of specific structural forms, including but not limited to annular ribs, cantilevered flexible arms with protruding detents, helical or bayonet-style twist-lock features, or ramped cam surfaces that translate axial movement into the necessary lateral deflection for engagement and disengagement of the locking features. The precise selection and arrangement of these locking surface types may be varied according to manufacturing preferences, desired tactile feedback during use, and durability requirements for repeated cycling of the device.

## Advantages of the Invention

The injection training device of the present invention offers numerous advantages over prior art training devices and safety syringe mechanisms. Principal among these advantages is the ability to reuse a single device across multiple training sessions and multiple trainees, substantially reducing the ongoing costs associated with injection training programs while simultaneously reducing the environmental impact and medical waste generated by disposable single-use training syringes.

Additionally, the automatic extension and locking of the shield following each simulated injection ensures a consistent and reliable safety mechanism that does not depend on the trainee remembering to manually engage a safety feature, thereby reducing the risk of accidental needle-stick or contact injuries during training exercises, particularly in high-volume training environments such as nursing schools, medical simulation centers, and continuing education programs for healthcare professionals.

The manual resetting feature further distinguishes this invention from conventional safety syringes, as it allows instructors or trainees to quickly and easily prepare the device for subsequent use without specialized tools or complex disassembly procedures, thereby facilitating efficient and continuous training sessions.

## Conclusion

Accordingly, the present invention provides a significant advancement in the field of medical training devices by delivering a reusable, safety-enhanced injection training device that automatically shields the injection simulation member after use while permitting straightforward manual resetting for repeated use, thereby addressing the longstanding need in the industry for cost-effective, safe, and sustainable training tools for injection technique instruction.

# Understanding Embodiments: What Happens After Resetting

In various technical and philosophical contexts, the concept of "embodiments" refers to specific implementations or manifestations of a broader idea, system, or invention. Understanding what occurs after a resetting process is crucial for evaluating how these embodiments function, adapt, and maintain their integrity over time.

## The Nature of Embodiments

An embodiment represents a concrete instance of an abstract concept. Whether in engineering, software design, or conceptual frameworks, embodiments serve as tangible expressions of theoretical principles. Each embodiment may vary slightly in its execution while still adhering to the core characteristics that define the overarching system or invention.

## The Resetting Process

Resetting is a fundamental operation across many systems—from electronic devices to organizational structures—that returns a state to its original or baseline configuration. This process often serves several purposes:

- **Clearing errors**: Removing accumulated faults or inconsistencies
- **Restoring defaults**: Returning to a known, stable starting point
- **Preparing for new input**: Creating a clean slate for subsequent operations
- **Maintaining reliability**: Ensuring consistent performance over extended use

## Life After Resetting

What happens after resetting is often the most critical phase in understanding an embodiment's functionality. Several key aspects typically emerge:

### 1. State Verification
Following a reset, systems typically undergo verification processes to confirm that the resetting was successful and that all parameters have returned to their expected baseline values.

### 2. Re-initialization
Many embodiments require a re-initialization sequence after resetting, where core functions are systematically restarted in a predetermined order to ensure proper operation.

### 3. Adaptive Response
Some sophisticated embodiments are designed to respond adaptively after resetting, incorporating learned behaviors or stored configurations that persist despite the reset, distinguishing between temporary states and permanent characteristics.

### 4. Continued Operation
Ultimately, the goal of resetting is to enable continued, improved operation. After resetting, an embodiment should ideally function more reliably, having shed any problematic states that necessitated the reset in the first place.

## Conclusion

The relationship between embodiments and the resetting process illustrates a fundamental principle in system design: the ability to return to a known state while preserving the capacity for continued, meaningful operation. Understanding what happens after resetting—whether in mechanical devices, software systems, or conceptual models—provides valuable insight into the resilience and adaptability inherent in well-designed embodiments. This cyclical process of operation, resetting, and renewed operation often defines the practical utility and longevity of any given implementation.

# Patent Abstract

**Reusable Injection Training Device with Auto-Resetting Spring-Loaded Safety Shield**

A reusable injection training device is disclosed for simulating needle-based injection procedures in medical and nursing education without risk of needlestick injury. The device comprises a housing configured to resemble a standard injection instrument, a retractable needle-simulating probe, and a spring-loaded safety shield mechanism disposed coaxially about the probe. Upon application of axial force simulating a skin-penetration event, the safety shield retracts into the housing, exposing the probe tip to simulate needle insertion. Following release of the applied force, an internal biasing spring automatically returns the safety shield to its extended, protective position, covering the probe tip and preventing inadvertent contact.

The device further includes a resettable actuation mechanism permitting repeated simulated injection cycles without manual reassembly, component replacement, or tool-assisted resetting, thereby enabling extended use across multiple training sessions and multiple trainees. In certain embodiments, the housing incorporates a visual or tactile feedback element, such as a colored indicator, audible click, or haptic response, to signal successful completion of a simulated injection stroke, enhancing procedural feedback for trainees. The device may further include an adjustable resistance mechanism to simulate varying tissue densities or injection depths.

The disclosed device provides a low-cost, durable, and reusable alternative to single-use or disposable training needles, reducing consumable waste and training costs while maintaining consistent safety standards. The invention is particularly suited for use in nursing schools, medical simulation centers, first-responder training programs, and continuing education courses for healthcare professionals.

# PATENT APPLICATION

## TITLE OF INVENTION
Medical Training Device Having Retractable Shield and Locking Mechanism for Simulating Injection Procedures

---

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present invention relates generally to medical training apparatus, and more particularly to a simulated injection device incorporating a plunger assembly, a retractable protective shield, and a locking mechanism configured to replicate the tactile feedback, operational sequence, and safety features of an actual hypodermic injection device for training purposes without capability of fluid delivery or needle penetration into tissue.

---

## BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

Medical training tools that simulate injection procedures are utilized to train healthcare practitioners, students, and caregivers in proper injection technique, including needle insertion angle, plunger depression rate, and post-injection safety protocols. Conventional training devices often fail to adequately replicate the mechanical resistance profiles, shield deployment mechanics, and locking engagement associated with modern safety-engineered injection devices, resulting in inadequate training transfer to real-world clinical practice. There exists a need for a reusable or single-use training device that accurately simulates these mechanical interactions while eliminating risk of accidental needlestick injury or fluid exposure.

---

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

In accordance with the purposes of the invention, as embodied and broadly described herein, the invention provides a medical training device comprising a barrel housing, a plunger assembly slidably disposed within the barrel housing, a retractable shield member movably coupled to a distal end of the barrel housing, and a locking mechanism configured to selectively engage the plunger assembly and/or the retractable shield member at one or more predetermined positions during a simulated injection cycle.

In one aspect, the plunger assembly is configured to translate axially within the barrel housing between a pre-injection position and a fully depressed position, wherein axial translation of the plunger assembly generates a resistance force simulating fluid injection resistance through a biasing element.

In another aspect, the retractable shield member is configured to translate between an extended position, in which a distal shield portion covers a simulated needle or needle-representative structure, and a retracted position, in which the simulated needle or needle-representative structure is exposed for training engagement with a training pad, mannequin, or other simulated tissue surface.

In yet another aspect, the locking mechanism comprises at least one engagement feature configured to releasably or irreversibly secure the retractable shield member in the extended position upon completion of the simulated injection cycle, thereby simulating a needlestick-prevention safety mechanism.

---

## BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS

**FIG. 1** is a perspective view of the medical training device in a pre-injection configuration, showing the retractable shield in an extended position.

**FIG. 2** is a cross-sectional side view of the medical training device illustrating the internal components of the plunger assembly, biasing element, and locking mechanism.

**FIG. 3** is a cross-sectional side view of the medical training device during a simulated injection, showing the retractable shield in a retracted position and the plunger assembly partially depressed.

**FIG. 4** is a cross-sectional side view of the medical training device following completion of the simulated injection cycle, showing the locking mechanism engaged and the retractable shield in the extended, locked position.

**FIG. 5** is an exploded view of the locking mechanism, illustrating the engagement feature, biasing member, and corresponding receiving structure.

---

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION

### General Architecture

Referring to FIGS. 1-4, the medical training device 100 comprises a barrel housing 110 defining a longitudinal axis A, a proximal end 112, and a distal end 114. The barrel housing 110 defines an internal bore 116 configured to slidably receive a plunger assembly 120. A retractable shield member 140 is movably coupled to the distal end 114 of the barrel housing 110 and is configured to translate along the longitudinal axis A between an extended position and a retracted position relative to a needle-representative structure 150 disposed at or near the distal end 114.

It will be understood that the needle-representative structure 150, in various embodiments, may comprise a blunt, non-penetrating simulated needle tip, a retractable stylus, or an entirely needle-free indicator structure configured to interface with a corresponding training surface without penetration capability, consistent with the training-only, non-clinical function of the device.

### Plunger Assembly

The plunger assembly 120 comprises a plunger rod 122 having a proximal thumb-engagement flange 124 and a distal piston element 126 slidably disposed within the internal bore 116 of the barrel housing 110. A biasing element 128, such as a compression spring or resilient elastomeric member, is disposed within the internal bore 116 and configured to exert a resistive force against the distal piston element 126 during axial translation of the plunger rod 122 from a proximal, pre-injection position to a distal, fully-depressed position.

In certain embodiments, the biasing element 128 is configured with a variable spring rate or a multi-stage resistance profile so as to simulate varying resistance encountered during different phases of an actual injection procedure, including initial breakaway resistance, sustained flow resistance, and end-of-dose resistance.

In certain embodiments, the plunger assembly 120 further comprises a dose-indicating structure 130, such as a graduated marking or an audible/tactile feedback element, configured to provide sensory feedback to a trainee corresponding to a simulated dosage volume delivered during axial translation of the plunger rod 122.

### Retractable Shield Member

The retractable shield member 140 comprises a shield body 142 defining a distal covering portion 144 and a proximal engagement portion 146. The shield body 142 is slidably or telescopically coupled to the barrel housing 110 such that the shield body 142 is configured to translate axially between:

(a) an extended position, wherein the distal covering portion 144 extends distally beyond the needle-representative structure 150 so as to substantially enclose the needle-representative structure 150; and

(b) a retracted position, wherein the distal covering portion 144 is displaced proximally relative to the extended position so as to expose the needle-representative structure 150 for simulated engagement with a training surface.

In certain embodiments, the retractable shield member 140 is biased toward the extended position by a shield-biasing element 148, such that upon removal of an axial displacing force applied to the shield body 142 during simulated tissue engagement, the shield body 142 automatically translates from the retracted position to the extended position.

### Locking Mechanism

Referring to FIG. 5, the locking mechanism 160 comprises an engagement feature 162 disposed on or within one of the barrel housing 110, the plunger assembly 120, or the retractable shield member 140, and a corresponding receiving structure 164 disposed on a corresponding one of the remaining components. The engagement feature 162 is configured to translate from a disengaged configuration to an engaged configuration in response to a triggering event, such as:

(i) full axial translation of the plunger rod 122 to the fully-depressed position;

(ii) axial translation of the retractable shield member 140 to the extended position following retraction; or

(iii) a combination of triggering events (i) and (ii).

In certain embodiments, the engagement feature 162 comprises a resilient locking tab configured to elastically deflect during translation of the corresponding component and to elastically return to a locked configuration upon alignment with the receiving structure 164, such as a locking recess or aperture, thereby producing an audible and/or tactile confirmation signal indicative of successful locking engagement.

In certain embodiments, the locking mechanism 160 is configured to irreversibly secure the retractable shield member 140 in the extended position following engagement, such that reverse axial translation of the shield body 142 from the extended position toward the retracted position is mechanically prevented, thereby simulating a single-use, needlestick-prevention safety feature characteristic of commercially available safety syringes.

In alternative embodiments, the locking mechanism 160 is configured to permit repeated engagement and disengagement cycles, such as through a resettable latch structure, so as to enable repeated reuse of the medical training device 100 for multiple training sessions.

### Optional Sensor and Feedback Integration

In certain embodiments, the medical training device 100 further comprises one or more sensors 170, such as a position sensor, force sensor, or optical encoder, disposed in operative communication with the plunger assembly 120 and/or the retractable shield member 140, and configured to generate signal data corresponding to at least one of: plunger translation velocity, plunger translation distance, shield retraction state, and locking mechanism engagement state. The medical training device 100 may further comprise a communication module configured to transmit the signal data to an external computing device for evaluation of trainee performance metrics, including injection speed, angle consistency (in embodiments incorporating an orientation sensor), and post-injection safety compliance.

---

## CLAIMS

# Resettable Injection Trainer with Automatic Shield Lock/Release Mechanism

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present invention relates generally to medical training devices, and more particularly to a resettable injection trainer apparatus incorporating a housing body, a plunger assembly, a simulated injection site, and an automatically actuating protective shield mechanism for repeated training use.

---

## BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

Medical, nursing, and paramedical training programs require repeated practice of injection techniques to develop proficiency, muscle memory, and procedural confidence in trainees. Traditional training solutions fall into several categories, each with notable limitations:

1. **Single-use training aids** that must be discarded after one or a limited number of uses, resulting in increased costs and waste for training institutions.

2. **Basic reusable models** lacking realistic mechanical feedback, such as the resistance and shield deployment behavior found in modern safety-engineered injection devices used in clinical practice.

3. **Devices without protective shielding**, which fail to train users in proper technique regarding needle safety shields now standard in clinical needle systems (e.g., safety syringes designed to reduce needlestick injuries).

There exists an unmet need for a training device that closely simulates the mechanical experience of using a modern safety syringe—including plunger depression, simulated tissue resistance, and automatic shield deployment upon withdrawal—while being fully resettable for repeated, cost-effective training use.

---

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The present invention provides a resettable injection trainer comprising:

(a) a **body** (housing) defining an internal cavity and supporting the operative components of the device;

(b) a **plunger** slidably disposed within the body, configured to simulate the depression force and travel of an actual syringe plunger;

(c) a **simulated injection site** disposed at or near a distal end of the body, configured to simulate tissue resistance and receive a simulated needle or probe; and

(d) a **shield** operatively coupled to the body and/or plunger via a locking and release mechanism, wherein the shield is configured to:
   - remain in a retracted or armed position during simulated injection,
   - automatically deploy to a locked, covering position upon withdrawal of the simulated needle or completion of the injection stroke, and
   - be manually reset to the armed position by an instructor or trainee for repeated use.

The invention thereby provides a realistic, reusable training platform that closely mimics the tactile and mechanical feedback of clinical safety syringes, while eliminating the cost and waste associated with single-use trainers.

---

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION

### 1. General Overview

Referring to the general construction of the device, the resettable injection trainer comprises four principal interacting subsystems: the body, the plunger, the simulated injection site, and the automatic shield mechanism. These components cooperate to replicate the sequence of a clinical injection procedure—insertion, depression, withdrawal, and shield deployment—in a manner suitable for repeated training exercises.

### 2. The Body

The body forms the primary structural housing of the trainer and may be fabricated from durable, cleanable, and preferably transparent or semi-transparent polymer material to allow visual observation of internal mechanisms for instructional purposes. The body defines:

- an elongated barrel portion configured to receive and guide the plunger;
- a distal coupling region configured to interface with the simulated injection site;
- one or more longitudinal channels, tracks, or rails configured to guide the shield between its armed (retracted) and deployed (locked) positions;
- optionally, one or more finger flanges or grip surfaces to facilitate handling during training.

In certain embodiments, the body further includes a viewing window or transparent section permitting observation of the internal locking mechanism, for pedagogical purposes.

### 3. The Plunger

The plunger is slidably received within the barrel of the body and is configured to translate axially in response to an applied thumb or hand force, simulating the depression stroke of an actual syringe plunger. The plunger may incorporate:

- a resistance-generating element (e.g., a spring, friction collar, elastomeric bushing, or calibrated damper) configured to simulate the force profile of injecting fluid into tissue;
- a plunger rod terminating in a thumb-press pad;
- an actuation feature (e.g., a cam surface, protrusion, or trigger tab) positioned to interact with the shield locking mechanism at or near the end of the plunger's forward stroke, such that full depression of the plunger arms the automatic shield release; and
- a return feature enabling the plunger to be manually withdrawn and reset following a training cycle, optionally assisted by a return spring.

### 4. The Simulated Injection Site

The simulated injection site is disposed at the distal end of the body and is configured to approximate the tactile resistance and feel of human or animal tissue during needle insertion. The simulated injection site may comprise:

- a replaceable or resettable elastomeric pad, membrane, gel insert, or synthetic tissue block, optionally self-sealing to permit repeated needle penetration without permanent damage;
- a receiving aperture or socket configured to align with a simulated needle or probe extending from or through the body; and
- optionally, sensors or indicator features (e.g., pressure switches, color-change materials, or electronic feedback elements) configured to provide feedback regarding injection angle, depth, or force to the trainee or instructor.

### 5. The Shield and Automatic Locking/Release Mechanism

The shield is a movable protective structure configured to selectively cover the simulated needle or injection interface. The shield is operatively coupled to the body via a locking and release mechanism comprising cooperating engagement features on the shield, plunger, and/or body, such that:

**(a) Armed (Retracted) State:** Prior to and during the simulated injection stroke, the shield is retained in a retracted position by a first locking feature (e.g., a detent, latch, or spring-loaded pawl), exposing the simulated needle or injection interface for use.

**(b) Automatic Release and Deployment:** Upon a triggering event—such as full depression of the plunger, withdrawal of the plunger past a predetermined position, or withdrawal of the simulated needle from the injection site—the first locking feature is disengaged, permitting a biasing element (e.g., a compression or torsion spring) to automatically drive the shield from the retracted position to a deployed, covering position over the simulated needle or injection interface.

**(c) Locked (Deployed) State:** Upon reaching the deployed position, a second locking feature engages to positively retain the shield in the covering position, preventing inadvertent retraction and simulating the "needlestick-safe" locked condition of clinical safety syringes.

**(d) Manual Reset:** The shield locking mechanism is further configured to permit manual disengagement of the second locking feature (e.g., via a reset button, release tab, key, or instructor-operated tool), allowing the shield to be manually retracted and re-armed by re-engaging the first locking feature, thereby preparing the device for a subsequent training cycle.

In various embodiments, the locking and release mechanism may be implemented using:
- spring-loaded ratchet and pawl arrangements;
- cam-and-follower systems actuated by plunger travel;
- magnetic detents;
- electromechanical actuators (e.g., a solenoid or motor-driven latch) controlled by a sensor detecting plunger position or needle withdrawal; or
- combinations of the foregoing.

### 6. Optional Features

Additional embodiments of the invention may incorporate:

- a **counter mechanism** to track the number of training cycles performed;
- **interchangeable simulated injection site inserts** representing different anatomical injection locations (e.g., deltoid, gluteal, ventrogluteal, subcutaneous abdominal sites);
- **audible or visual feedback** (e.g., a click, tone, or light) indicating correct shield deployment and locking;
- a **modular simulated needle assembly** permitting replacement of the needle-simulating component independent of the shield and plunger assembly; and
- **connectivity features** enabling the device to interface with an external training-assessment system (e.g., via Bluetooth or wired connection) to log performance data such as injection force, angle, and shield deployment timing.

---

## CLAIMS (Illustrative)

**1.** A resettable injection trainer comprising:
   a body defining an internal cavity;
   a plunger slidably disposed within the body;
   a simulated injection site disposed at a distal end of the body; and
   a shield operatively coupled to the body, the shield being movable between a retracted position and a deployed position;
   wherein the shield is configured to automatically move from the retracted position to the deployed position in response to a triggering event associated with operation of the plunger or withdrawal from the simulated injection site, and to lock in the deployed position; and
   wherein the shield is further configured to be manually reset from the deployed position to the retracted position for repeated use of the trainer.

**2.** The trainer of claim 1, wherein the triggering event comprises full depression of the plunger within the body.

**3.** The trainer of claim 1, wherein the shield is biased toward the deployed position by a spring, and is retained in the retracted position by a releasable first locking feature.

**4.** The trainer of claim 1, further comprising a second locking feature configured to retain the shield in the deployed position until manually released.

**5.** The trainer of claim 1, wherein the simulated injection site comprises a replaceable, self-sealing elastomeric insert configured to simulate tissue resistance upon repeated needle insertion.

**6.** The trainer of claim 1, wherein the plunger includes a resistance-generating element configured to simulate injection force feedback.

**7.** The trainer of claim 1, further comprising a counter configured to record a number of completed training cycles.

**8.** The trainer of claim 1, wherein the body includes a transparent portion permitting visual observation of the shield locking mechanism during operation.

**9.** The trainer of claim 1, further comprising a sensor configured to detect plunger position or shield state, and to communicate corresponding data to an external device.

**10.** A method of using the resettable injection trainer of claim 1, comprising:
   arming the shield in the retracted position;
   inserting a simulated needle into the simulated injection site;
   depressing the plunger to simulate fluid delivery;
   withdrawing the simulated needle, thereby triggering automatic deployment and locking of the shield; and
   manually resetting the shield to the retracted position to prepare the trainer for a subsequent use.

---

## ADVANTAGES OF THE INVENTION

- Provides realistic simulation of modern safety syringe mechanics, including automatic needle-shielding behavior;
- Enables repeated, cost-effective training through a fully resettable design;
- Reduces training material waste compared to single-use trainers;
- Enhances trainee safety awareness by reinforcing correct handling of automatic shield-equipped clinical devices;
- Adaptable to multiple training contexts through interchangeable injection site inserts and optional data-logging features.

---

For actual patent prosecution, claims and specification would need to be refined by a registered patent practitioner in consultation with the inventor(s), and a formal prior art search should be conducted prior to filing.*

# Patent Summary

## Title
**Injection Training Device with Automatically Deployable and Manually Resettable Needle Shield Mechanism**

## Field of the Invention
The present disclosure relates to medical training devices, and more particularly to a simulated injection apparatus incorporating a safety shield mechanism configured to automatically cover a needle simulator following a simulated injection procedure, wherein the shield mechanism is manually resettable to permit repeated training use.

## Background
Training devices for injection technique instruction typically employ a needle simulator—a blunt or retractable structure mimicking a hypodermic needle—to allow trainees to practice injection procedures without risk of injury. Conventional training devices, however, often fail to replicate modern needle-safety features now standard in clinical practice, such as passive needle-shielding mechanisms that automatically cover a needle tip after use to prevent accidental needlestick injury. Existing training tools that do incorporate such shields are frequently single-use or require disassembly for reset, limiting their utility in repeated classroom or clinical training settings.

There exists a need for an injection training device that faithfully simulates the automatic deployment of a needle safety shield, while also allowing the shield to be manually reset by an instructor or trainee for continued reuse.

## Summary of the Invention

In accordance with the present disclosure, an injection training device is provided comprising:

1. **A housing** defining a body portion configured to be grasped in a manner similar to a hypodermic syringe or injection pen device;

2. **A needle simulator** disposed at a distal end of the housing, the needle simulator being a blunt-tipped or non-piercing structure configured to simulate the visual and tactile characteristics of a hypodermic needle during a training injection procedure;

3. **A shield mechanism** slidably or pivotably coupled to the housing, the shield mechanism being biased toward a deployed position by a biasing element (e.g., a spring), wherein:
   - the shield mechanism is retained in a retracted position during simulated use, exposing the needle simulator;
   - upon completion of a simulated injection (e.g., upon release of an actuation button, removal of axial pressure, or retraction of a plunger simulator), the shield mechanism is automatically driven by the biasing element to a deployed position in which it extends distally to substantially or fully enclose the needle simulator, thereby simulating a passive needle-safety shielding event;

4. **A locking element** configured to releasably retain the shield mechanism in the deployed position following automatic actuation, preventing unintended retraction during handling; and

5. **A manual reset mechanism** operable by a user to disengage the locking element and return the shield mechanism to the retracted position against the bias of the biasing element, thereby readying the device for a subsequent simulated injection cycle.

In certain embodiments, the manual reset mechanism comprises a reset button, lever, or rotatable collar accessible from an exterior surface of the housing. In other embodiments, the reset mechanism may require a two-step or dual-action input (e.g., simultaneous depression and rotation) to reduce the likelihood of accidental resetting, further enhancing training realism.

The device may further include one or more sensors or mechanical indicators configured to detect and/or signal successful shield deployment, such as an audible click, haptic feedback, or visual indicator, for instructional feedback purposes.

## Advantages
The disclosed device provides significant advantages over prior training tools, including:
- Realistic simulation of modern passive needle-safety mechanisms used in clinical injection devices;
- Repeatable use through a manually resettable shield mechanism, reducing training costs and device turnover;
- Enhanced trainee familiarity with safety-engineered injection devices prior to clinical use with live patients;
- Reduced risk of injury during training due to the non-piercing needle simulator combined with the shielding function.

## Brief Description of Alternative Embodiments
Alternative embodiments may include interchangeable needle simulator tips of varying gauge appearance, adjustable shield deployment resistance to simulate different device models, and modular housings compatible with multiple injection-device form factors (e.g., syringe, auto-injector, or injection pen simulators).

# DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF EMBODIMENTS

The following embodiments describe various implementations of a training injection pen having a needle shield (or simulated needle shield) that is selectively locked and released through mechanical interaction with axial movement of an internal plunger. It is understood that these embodiments are illustrative and non-limiting, and that features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features of another embodiment unless expressly stated otherwise.

## Embodiment 1: General Pen Structure

In one embodiment, the training injection pen (100) comprises a housing (110) defining a proximal end and a distal end, a plunger (120) slidably disposed within the housing and configured to move axially between a retracted position and an extended position, a shield (130) movably coupled to the distal end of the housing, and a locking mechanism (140) operatively connecting the plunger (120) to the shield (130). The shield (130) is configured to cover a simulated needle or needle-free tip (150) disposed at the distal end of the housing when the shield is in a locked, extended configuration, and to expose the simulated needle or tip when the shield is retracted.

In this embodiment, the locking mechanism (140) comprises one or more locking members (142) that engage corresponding recesses or detents (144) formed in an inner surface of the shield (130). The locking members (142) are biased radially outward by a spring element (146) such that, in a default state, the locking members engage the detents (144) and prevent axial movement of the shield (130) relative to the housing (110).

## Embodiment 2: Plunger-Actuated Release

In another embodiment, the plunger (120) includes a cam surface (122) or tapered profile positioned along its length such that, upon depression of the plunger from the retracted position toward the extended position, the cam surface (122) contacts an actuating arm (148) coupled to the locking members (142). Continued axial movement of the plunger causes the actuating arm (148) to displace the locking members (142) radially inward, disengaging them from the detents (144) of the shield (130) and thereby releasing the shield for axial movement relative to the housing (110).

In a further aspect of this embodiment, the cam surface (122) is positioned such that release of the locking members (142) occurs only after the plunger (120) has traveled a predetermined distance corresponding to a simulated dose delivery, such that the shield (130) remains locked during an initial portion of the plunger stroke and is released only near or at the end of the stroke, simulating the sequence of an actual injection device.

## Embodiment 3: Spring-Biased Shield Retraction

In a further embodiment, the shield (130) is coupled to a shield-biasing spring (132) disposed between the housing (110) and the shield (130), the shield-biasing spring (132) being configured to urge the shield toward the extended, covering position. When the locking members (142) are disengaged by the actuating arm (148) as described above, the shield-biasing spring (132) drives the shield (130) distally to cover the simulated needle or tip (150) automatically, without requiring manual manipulation by the user.

In an alternative configuration of this embodiment, the shield-biasing spring (132) is configured to urge the shield (130) proximally upon release, exposing the simulated needle tip (150) rather than covering it, such that the training pen simulates a device in which the shield retracts upon dose completion.

## Embodiment 4: Reversible Locking Upon Plunger Retraction

In another embodiment, the locking mechanism (140) is configured to re-engage the locking members (142) with the shield (130) upon retraction of the plunger (120) back to its initial, retracted position. In this embodiment, a return spring (124) is disposed to bias the plunger (120) toward the retracted position, and the actuating arm (148) is configured such that, as the plunger returns, the cam surface (122) disengages from the actuating arm (148), allowing the locking members (142), under bias from spring element (146), to move radially outward and re-engage the detents (144) of the shield (130), thereby locking the shield in its current axial position.

This embodiment allows the training pen to be reset for repeated simulated injection cycles, with the shield locking and unlocking synchronized to plunger movement in a manner that mimics single-use or reusable injection devices.

## Embodiment 5: Multi-Stage Locking Mechanism

In a further embodiment, the locking mechanism (140) comprises a multi-stage detent arrangement, wherein the shield (130) includes a first detent (144a) corresponding to a fully extended, locked position and a second detent (144b) corresponding to a partially retracted position. In this embodiment, the locking members (142) are configured to sequentially engage the first detent (144a) and the second detent (144b) as the plunger (120) moves through corresponding stages of its stroke, such that the shield (130) is released in discrete steps rather than in a single continuous motion.

This staged release may be used, for example, to simulate multi-phase injection sequences, such as a priming stage followed by a full dose delivery stage, or to provide tactile and audible feedback (e.g., a "click") at each stage of shield movement.

## Embodiment 6: Sensor-Based Electronic Locking

In an alternative embodiment, the locking mechanism (140) is electromechanical rather than purely mechanical. In this embodiment, the pen (100) includes a position sensor (160), such as a Hall-effect sensor, optical encoder, or potentiometer, configured to detect the axial position of the plunger (120). The position sensor (160) is in communication with a controller (170), which is operatively connected to an electromechanical actuator (180), such as a solenoid or motor-driven latch, coupled to the locking members (142) or directly to the shield (130).

In this embodiment, when the position sensor (160) detects that the plunger (120) has reached a predetermined position corresponding to a simulated dose delivery, the controller (170) sends a signal to the electromechanical actuator (180) to release the locking members (142) or shield (130). This embodiment enables programmable or adjustable locking thresholds, and may further include a feedback module (190), such as an LED indicator, speaker, or haptic element, configured to provide sensory feedback to the user upon shield release, plunger depression, or completion of the simulated injection.

## Embodiment 7: Shield with Visual Indicator

In another embodiment, the shield (130) includes a visual indicator (152), such as a colored band, printed marking, or window, that becomes visible to the user only when the shield (130) is in the released and/or fully extended position. This visual indicator (152) provides confirmation to a trainee that the simulated injection sequence has been properly completed and that the shield (130) has moved into its intended terminal position.

## Embodiment 8: Adjustable Locking Threshold

In a further embodiment, the training pen (100) includes an adjustment mechanism (200) configured to vary the axial position along the plunger's (120) stroke at which the cam surface (122) engages the actuating arm (148), thereby allowing the point of shield release to be adjusted. The adjustment mechanism (200) may comprise, for example, a rotatable collar, a sliding insert, or a set of interchangeable cam elements, allowing the training pen (100) to simulate injection devices having different dose volumes or different shield-release timings.

## Embodiment 9: Removable/Replaceable Shield Assembly

In yet another embodiment, the shield (130) and its associated locking components (142, 144, 146) are provided as a removable and replaceable cartridge or module (210), configured to detachably couple to the distal end of the housing (110). This embodiment permits the training pen (100) to be reconfigured with shields of differing lengths, shapes, or locking characteristics, for example, to simulate different commercially available injection pen products, or to replace worn components after repeated training use.

## Embodiment 10: Combination with Dose-Setting Mechanism

In a further embodiment, the training pen (100) further includes a dose-setting mechanism (220), such as a rotatable dial coupled to the plunger (120) via a threaded interface, configured to allow a user to select a simulated dose amount prior to actuation. In this embodiment, the axial travel distance required to trigger release of the shield-locking mechanism (140) corresponds to the dose amount selected via the dose-setting mechanism (220), such that the plunger (120) must travel a distance proportional to the selected dose before the locking members (142) are disengaged from the shield (130).

---

It will be appreciated by those skilled in the art that the above embodiments may be modified, combined, or substituted with equivalent structures without departing from the scope of the invention. For example, the locking members (142) may be implemented as pins, balls, tabs, or flexible fingers; the biasing elements described herein may be implemented using coil springs, leaf springs, elastomeric elements, or magnetic biasing; and the "shield" (130) may take the form of a sliding sleeve, a hinged cover, or a rotatable cap, without departing from the underlying principle of plunger-actuated locking and release.
